proposal.readme_text:
STRspy2.0: Unlocking the Potential of Long Reads for Forensic DNA Profiling.

# NEWS: We are excited to announce the new release of STRspy, version 2.0. ( https://github.com/unique379r/strspy/tree/STRspy2.0 ) ## Whats New in STRspy2.0 ### 1. DB_v2: Autosome and ChrY-specific STRs (comprehensive STR database from GenBank records in the STRSeq BioProject (accessions: PRJNA380345 and PRJNA380347)) ### 2. New Utility script to generate DB from Genebank and Fasta. ### 3. New Interface of command line options from main scripts ### 4. New Benchmarking results with multiple datasets including Case Samples ## Cite

Hall CL, Kesharwani RK, Phillips NR, Planz JV, Sedlazeck FJ, Zascavage RR. Accurate profiling of forensic autosomal STRs using the Oxford Nanopore Technologies MinION device. Forensic Sci Int Genet. 2022 Jan;56:102629. doi: 10.1016/j.fsigen.2021.102629. Epub 2021 Nov 17. PMID: 34837788. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34837788/

## Latest Publication

Hall, C.L.; Kesharwani, R.K.; McBroom Henson, K.E.; Kapema, B.; Phillips, N.R.; Sedlazeck, F.J.; Zascavage, R.R. STRspy2.0: Unlocking the Potential of Long Reads for Forensic DNA Profiling. Int. J. Mol. Sci. 2026, 27, 1889. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms27041889

# STRspy2.0 ![](figs/fig1.png)

Figure 1. Schematic overview of STRspy2.0 workflow. (a) STRspy2.0 relies on an STR allele database to generate profiles consistent with established length-based forensic nomenclature. Users can use the STRspy2.0 database or build their own from GenBank records. When GenBank records are provided, STRspy2.0 automatically generates database entries using the locus name, reference chromosome, repeat location, repeat sequence, and flanking sequence variants, then adds 500 bp flanks from hg38 to each allele. (b) During data analysis, STRspy2.0 aligns reads to the human reference genome, extracts those overlapping STR loci, and realigns them to the STR allele database. Each allele is ranked by normalized read count to determine the genotype at each locus.

## Abstract

Forensic human identification relies on length-based differences in short tandem repeats (STRs) across autosomal and Y chromosomes, which require separate reactions and provide limited resolution. While next-generation sequencing offers greater discriminatory power, most platforms are expensive and restricted to traditional lab settings. Nanopore sequencing has the potential to change this with the real-time, portable MinION sequencer. However, forensic-specific tools that generate STR profiles compatible with established length-based databases are lacking. To address this, we developed STRspy2.0, which simultaneously profiles autosomal and Y-STRs using nanopore reads. STRspy2.0 produced accurate profiles for 54 multiplexed control libraries and 41 mock casework samples (blood, swab, bone), achieving overall F1-scores of 100% and 99.75%, respectively. It maintains compatibility with existing forensic databases while providing higher resolution than traditional profiles. Our updated method and comprehensive database, along with the MinION’s small size and price, make sequence-based STR profiling more accessible to forensic laboratories and resource-limited settings..

## Key Features 1. Input either fastq (raw reads usually from ONT) or bam (pre-aligned reads by user) 2. Reports raw counts of allele and Normalized counts by their maximum value 3. Find the top two significant Alleles (filtering threshold set by the user such as 0.4) 4. Now also detect top one for Y-STR. 4. Detects Small variants such as SNP and Indels 5. Reports mapping summary and STR region of overlaps 6. Stutters analysis for simple motifs of STRs ## Installation STRspy v2.0 requires Conda (for example [Miniconda](https://docs.conda.io/en/latest/miniconda.html) or Miniforge) and the tools declared in `setup/STRspy_2.0_env.yml` (`gnu parallel >=20210222`, `samtools >=v1.12`, `bedtools >=v2.30.0`, `minimap2 >=v2.18-r1015`, `xatlas >=v0.3`, `seqkit >=v2.4.0`). ### Clone the repository ```bash git clone https://github.com/Tfronta/strspy.git cd strspy ``` This is the fork with the corrections described on this page, and its default branch is the one you want, so no `--branch` is needed. The upstream repository is at https://github.com/unique379r/strspy, where `STRspy2.0` is a branch and `main` still holds version 1.0. ### Create an environment ```bash conda env create -f setup/STRspy_2.0_env.yml conda activate strspy_env ``` `config/UserToolsConfig.txt` already reads the six tools from `PATH` while `strspy_env` is active. If you install dependencies outside that environment and need absolute paths written into `config/UserToolsConfig.txt`, run `bash setup/GenerateToolConfig.sh` from the repository root with your environment active. Keep the environment active while you run STRspy: the scripts call `sed -i` in its GNU form, and on macOS only the `sed` from the environment accepts it. ## Database: use STRspy2.0-DB-fixed (important) The prebuilt `db-v2/STRspy2.0-DB.zip`, and databases built with `BuildDB_From_GeneBank.V1.sh`, contain FASTA files named `mod.fa` or `mod1.fa` that STRspy does not read, because it looks for `.fa`. With the unmodified zip, TPOX, FGA, D5S818, D7S820, D8S1179, D10S1248, D12S391 and D13S317 get no reads at all, and some alleles of DYS385ab, DYS390 and DYS458 are never considered. The run can still complete without an error, so the affected loci are simply missing from the results. This fork ships a corrected database that you can use directly: - `db-v2/STRspy2.0-DB-fixed/` (`.bed`, `.fa` and `.fai` files for each locus) To fix your own copy of the database instead (for example one built with BuildDB), unzip it, make the folder writable and run the merge script. samtools is needed to rebuild the `.fai` indexes. ```bash unzip db-v2/STRspy2.0-DB.zip -d my_db chmod -R u+w my_db bash db-v2/optional-create-custom-db/fix_db_names.sh my_db/STRspy2.0-DB ``` The script merges each `mod*.fa` into `.fa` without duplicating records, so no alleles are lost, and it is safe to run more than once. ## Quickstart 1. Edit `config/InputConfig.txt` so that it describes your data (every field is explained below). 2. With the environment active, run `bash setup/GenerateToolConfig.sh` from the repository root, so that `config/UserToolsConfig.txt` holds the paths of the tools you are actually using. 3. Create the output directory named in `OUTPUT_DIR`: the run stops if it does not already exist. Step 2 matters more than it looks. In the original STRspy a path that does not exist stops nothing. Each call to the tool fails on its own line, the run still ends with `#Done.` and exit status 0, and the tables under `Results/Countings/` come out empty, so the affected loci look as though they had no reads. In this fork the core scripts read the paths before they start and stop with the list of tools they cannot run, and `GenerateToolConfig.sh` stops rather than write a path it could not find. The file shipped here reads the tools from `PATH`, so it works while the environment is active; step 2 replaces it with absolute paths, which is what a wrapper script or a job scheduler needs. ## Run STRspy Run the core script directly from the repository root on an aligned BAM file: ```bash bash src/STRspy_Normal_v2.0_Args.sh -i sample.bam -r yes -t ont -f db-v2/STRspy2.0-DB-fixed -b db-v2/STRspy2.0-DB-fixed -l db-v2/STRspy_v2.DB.sort.bed -k 0.4 -o Results -c config/UserToolsConfig.txt -d 4 ``` Alternatively, you can pass a directory of `.bam` (`-r yes`) or `.fastq.gz` (`-r no`) files via `-i`, or use the config-based wrapper (`bash ./STRspy_run_v2.0_Args.sh -i config/InputConfig.txt -t config/UserToolsConfig.txt -j normal` after editing `config/InputConfig.txt`). ## InputConfig.txt INPUT_DIR : A dir must have either fastq (Oxford nanopore genomic reads) or bam (aligned genomic reads such as from PacBio) INPUT_BAM : Given inputs are bam or fastq (yes or no) READ_TYPE : Sequencing Technology (ont or pb) STR_FASTA : A dir contains Fasta files for each STR region of interest [assimung it has flanking regions (+/-) of 500bp] STR_BED : A dir contains Bed files for each STR region of interest [assimung it has flanking regions (+/-) of 500bp] GENOME_FASTA: Genome fasta (hg19/hg38) must provide in case of fastq input. REGION_BED : All STr\R bed has to concatenate into a single bed file to calculate the coverage of it from the alignment sample file. NORM_CUTOFF : A normalization threshold is required to select the top two allles of a STR OUTPUT_DIR : A empty directory to write the results THREADS : Number of memory should be used (default = 1) ## ToolsConfig.txt `GenerateToolConfig.sh` writes this file, so there is normally no reason to edit it by hand. Each value is read with `grep` and `cut -d '='`, so it has to follow the `=` with no space or tab around it: earlier versions of this page showed the names padded with tabs, which leaves the tab inside the path and the tool is then not found. `SEQKIT` is written for completeness and is not read by the core scripts. ``` BEDTOOLS=/user/path/bedtools MINIMAP=/user/path/minimap2 SAMTOOLS=/user/path/samtools XATLAS=/user/path/xatlas PARALLEL=/user/path/parallel SEQKIT=/user/path/seqkit ``` ## Getting help **bash strspy/STRspy_run_v2.0_Args.sh -h** ``` _____ _______ _____ / ____|__ __| __ \ | (___ | | | |__) |___ _ __ _ _ \___ \ | | | _ // __| '_ \| | | | ____) | | | | | \ \\__ \ |_) | |_| | |_____/ |_| |_| \_\___/ .__/ \__, | | | __/ | |_| |___/ =============================================== _ _ __ __ _ _____ _______ _____ __ _ _ _ /\ | | | | / _| / _| (_) / ____|__ __| __ \ / _(_) (_) / \ | |_ ___ ___ | | | |_ ___ _ __ | |_ ___ _ __ ___ _ __ ___ _ ___ | (___ | | | |__) | _ __ _ __ ___ | |_ _| |_ _ __ __ _ / /\ \ | __/ _ \ / _ \| | | _/ _ \| '__| | _/ _ \| '__/ _ \ '_ \/ __| |/ __| \___ \ | | | _ / | '_ \| '__/ _ \| _| | | | '_ \ / _` | / ____ \ | || (_) | (_) | | | || (_) | | | || (_) | | | __/ | | \__ \ | (__ ____) | | | | | \ \ | |_) | | | (_) | | | | | | | | | (_| | /_/ \_\ \__\___/ \___/|_| |_| \___/|_| |_| \___/|_| \___|_| |_|___/_|\___| |_____/ |_| |_| \_\ | .__/|_| \___/|_| |_|_|_|_| |_|\__, | | | __/ | |_| |___/ #^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^Welcome to STRspy^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^# # Analysis : Finding forensic STRs in a Long Read Sample # Requested Citation : https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fsigen.2021.102629 # Author : bioinforupesh2009 DOT au AT gmail DOT com # Copyright (c) : 2021 Kesharwani RK #^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^# Usage: bash STRspy_run_v2.0_Args.sh [-h] [-i -t -j] -- This script is wrapper of STRspy [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fsigen.2021.102629] where: -h show the help -i input config (InputConfig.txt) -t tools config (ToolsConfig.txt) -j job type (parallel/normal) [default: normal] ``` ### Core scripts **bash strspy/src/STRspy_Normal_v2.0_Args.sh -h** ``` #^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^Welcome to STRspy^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^# # Analysis : Finding forensic STRs in a Long Read Sample # Requested Citation : https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms27041889 # Author : bioinforupesh2009 DOT au AT gmail DOT com # Copyright (c) : 2026 Kesharwani RK #^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^# Usage: bash STRspy_Normal_v2.0_Args.sh [-h] [-s -r -t -f -b -g -l -k -o -c -d] -- This script is core-method of STRspy2.0 [https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms27041889] where: -h show the help -s input read dir (either bam or fastq) -r is input bam? (yes/no) -t technology type (ont/pb) -f dir of database fasta -b dir of database bed -g genome fasta file (fa) -l a file of known regions (bed) -k cutoff to find top two alleles (Any value from 0.1 to 0.9) [default: 0.4] -o results dir -c a file of tools config -d Number of threads to use ``` **bash strspy/src/STRspy_Parallel_v2.0_Args.sh -h** ``` #^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^Welcome to STRspy^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^# # Analysis : Finding forensic STRs in a Long Read Sample # Requested Citation : https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms27041889 # Author : bioinforupesh2009 DOT au AT gmail DOT com # Copyright (c) : 2026 Kesharwani RK #^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^# Usage: bash STRspy_Parallel_v2.0_Args.sh [-h] [-s -r -t -f -b -g -l -k -o -c] -- This script is core-method of STRspy2.0 [https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms27041889] where: -h show the help -s input read dir (either bam or fastq) -r is input bam? (yes/no) -t technology type (ont/pb) -f dir of database fasta -b dir of database bed -g genome fasta file (fa) -l a file of known regions (bed) -k cutoff to find top two alleles (Any value from 0.1 to 0.9) [default: 0.4] -o results dir -c a file of tools config -d Num of Threads ``` ## Results from the publication ![](figs/fig2.png)

Figure 2. Read mapping statistics for MinION sequencing runs. Bar plots showing the proportion of passed reads that were STR-mapped (on-target), off-target, and unmapped for the (a), control multiplexes and (b), casework-relevant samples. Each plot shows samples loaded onto a single MinION flow cell. Libraries in the control multiplex are labeled according to sample letter and barcode. A (NIST A), B (NIST B), C (NIST C), M (2800 M).

![](figs/fig3.png)

Figure 3. STRspy2.0 can resolve isoalleles within and between individuals. Allelic balance for autosomal and Y-STR isoalleles detected across control samples in the multiplexing experiment. Each colored bar represents a distinct sequence-based isoallele. Isoallele pairs are shown as blue/orange (pair 1) and green/pink (pair 2) for each locus. Heterozygous alleles that are not in the isoallele pair are colored grey, and samples without isoalleles at a given locus are not shown. Libraries are labeled according to sample letter, barcode, and multiplex size. A (NIST A), B (NIST B), C (NIST C), and M (2800 M).

![](figs/fig4.png)

Figure 4. STRspy2.0 can resolve isoalleles in challenging casework-relevant samples. Normalized read counts for sequence-based alleles detected at D2S1338, D3S1358, and D21S11 in one bone sample (bone03). The red dashed line indicates the normalization threshold (0.4) used to detect heterozygous alleles.

## Author Contributions C.L.H. and R.K.K. are co-first authors. C.L.H. performed the ONT and Illumina sequencing and contributed most of the manuscript text and figures. R.K.K. performed data analysis, including the updates to STRspy, and contributed to the results presented in the manuscript. K.E.M.H. interpreted data and was a contributor in writing the manuscript. STRspy2.0: Unlocking the Potential of Long Reads for Forensic DNA Profiling.

# NEWS: We are excited to announce the new release of STRspy, version 2.0. ( https://github.com/unique379r/strspy/tree/STRspy2.0 ) ## Whats New in STRspy2.0 ### 1. DB_v2: Autosome and ChrY-specific STRs (comprehensive STR database from GenBank records in the STRSeq BioProject (accessions: PRJNA380345 and PRJNA380347)) ### 2. New Utility script to generate DB from Genebank and Fasta. ### 3. New Interface of command line options from main scripts ### 4. New Benchmarking results with multiple datasets including Case Samples ## Cite

Hall CL, Kesharwani RK, Phillips NR, Planz JV, Sedlazeck FJ, Zascavage RR. Accurate profiling of forensic autosomal STRs using the Oxford Nanopore Technologies MinION device. Forensic Sci Int Genet. 2022 Jan;56:102629. doi: 10.1016/j.fsigen.2021.102629. Epub 2021 Nov 17. PMID: 34837788. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34837788/

## Latest Publication

Hall, C.L.; Kesharwani, R.K.; McBroom Henson, K.E.; Kapema, B.; Phillips, N.R.; Sedlazeck, F.J.; Zascavage, R.R. STRspy2.0: Unlocking the Potential of Long Reads for Forensic DNA Profiling. Int. J. Mol. Sci. 2026, 27, 1889. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms27041889

# STRspy2.0 ![](figs/fig1.png)

Figure 1. Schematic overview of STRspy2.0 workflow. (a) STRspy2.0 relies on an STR allele database to generate profiles consistent with established length-based forensic nomenclature. Users can use the STRspy2.0 database or build their own from GenBank records. When GenBank records are provided, STRspy2.0 automatically generates database entries using the locus name, reference chromosome, repeat location, repeat sequence, and flanking sequence variants, then adds 500 bp flanks from hg38 to each allele. (b) During data analysis, STRspy2.0 aligns reads to the human reference genome, extracts those overlapping STR loci, and realigns them to the STR allele database. Each allele is ranked by normalized read count to determine the genotype at each locus.

## Abstract

Forensic human identification relies on length-based differences in short tandem repeats (STRs) across autosomal and Y chromosomes, which require separate reactions and provide limited resolution. While next-generation sequencing offers greater discriminatory power, most platforms are expensive and restricted to traditional lab settings. Nanopore sequencing has the potential to change this with the real-time, portable MinION sequencer. However, forensic-specific tools that generate STR profiles compatible with established length-based databases are lacking. To address this, we developed STRspy2.0, which simultaneously profiles autosomal and Y-STRs using nanopore reads. STRspy2.0 produced accurate profiles for 54 multiplexed control libraries and 41 mock casework samples (blood, swab, bone), achieving overall F1-scores of 100% and 99.75%, respectively. It maintains compatibility with existing forensic databases while providing higher resolution than traditional profiles. Our updated method and comprehensive database, along with the MinION’s small size and price, make sequence-based STR profiling more accessible to forensic laboratories and resource-limited settings..

## Key Features 1. Input either fastq (raw reads usually from ONT) or bam (pre-aligned reads by user) 2. Reports raw counts of allele and Normalized counts by their maximum value 3. Find the top two significant Alleles (filtering threshold set by the user such as 0.4) 4. Now also detect top one for Y-STR. 4. Detects Small variants such as SNP and Indels 5. Reports mapping summary and STR region of overlaps 6. Stutters analysis for simple motifs of STRs ## Installation STRspy v2.0 requires Conda (for example [Miniconda](https://docs.conda.io/en/latest/miniconda.html) or Miniforge) and the tools declared in `setup/STRspy_2.0_env.yml` (`gnu parallel >=20210222`, `samtools >=v1.12`, `bedtools >=v2.30.0`, `minimap2 >=v2.18-r1015`, `xatlas >=v0.3`, `seqkit >=v2.4.0`). ### Clone the repository ```bash git clone https://github.com/Tfronta/strspy.git cd strspy ``` This is the fork with the corrections described on this page, and its default branch is the one you want, so no `--branch` is needed. The upstream repository is at https://github.com/unique379r/strspy, where `STRspy2.0` is a branch and `main` still holds version 1.0. ### Create an environment ```bash conda env create -f setup/STRspy_2.0_env.yml conda activate strspy_env ``` `config/UserToolsConfig.txt` already reads the six tools from `PATH` while `strspy_env` is active. If you install dependencies outside that environment and need absolute paths written into `config/UserToolsConfig.txt`, run `bash setup/GenerateToolConfig.sh` from the repository root with your environment active. Keep the environment active while you run STRspy: the scripts call `sed -i` in its GNU form, and on macOS only the `sed` from the environment accepts it. ## Database: use STRspy2.0-DB-fixed (important) The prebuilt `db-v2/STRspy2.0-DB.zip`, and databases built with `BuildDB_From_GeneBank.V1.sh`, contain FASTA files named `mod.fa` or `mod1.fa` that STRspy does not read, because it looks for `.fa`. With the unmodified zip, TPOX, FGA, D5S818, D7S820, D8S1179, D10S1248, D12S391 and D13S317 get no reads at all, and some alleles of DYS385ab, DYS390 and DYS458 are never considered. The run can still complete without an error, so the affected loci are simply missing from the results. This fork ships a corrected database that you can use directly: - `db-v2/STRspy2.0-DB-fixed/` (`.bed`, `.fa` and `.fai` files for each locus) To fix your own copy of the database instead (for example one built with BuildDB), unzip it, make the folder writable and run the merge script. samtools is needed to rebuild the `.fai` indexes. ```bash unzip db-v2/STRspy2.0-DB.zip -d my_db chmod -R u+w my_db bash db-v2/optional-create-custom-db/fix_db_names.sh my_db/STRspy2.0-DB ``` The script merges each `mod*.fa` into `.fa` without duplicating records, so no alleles are lost, and it is safe to run more than once. ## Quickstart 1. Edit `config/InputConfig.txt` so that it describes your data (every field is explained below). 2. With the environment active, run `bash setup/GenerateToolConfig.sh` from the repository root, so that `config/UserToolsConfig.txt` holds the paths of the tools you are actually using. 3. Create the output directory named in `OUTPUT_DIR`: the run stops if it does not already exist. Step 2 matters more than it looks. In the original STRspy a path that does not exist stops nothing. Each call to the tool fails on its own line, the run still ends with `#Done.` and exit status 0, and the tables under `Results/Countings/` come out empty, so the affected loci look as though they had no reads. In this fork the core scripts read the paths before they start and stop with the list of tools they cannot run, and `GenerateToolConfig.sh` stops rather than write a path it could not find. The file shipped here reads the tools from `PATH`, so it works while the environment is active; step 2 replaces it with absolute paths, which is what a wrapper script or a job scheduler needs. ## Run STRspy Run the core script directly from the repository root on an aligned BAM file: ```bash bash src/STRspy_Normal_v2.0_Args.sh -i sample.bam -r yes -t ont -f db-v2/STRspy2.0-DB-fixed -b db-v2/STRspy2.0-DB-fixed -l db-v2/STRspy_v2.DB.sort.bed -k 0.4 -o Results -c config/UserToolsConfig.txt -d 4 ``` Alternatively, you can pass a directory of `.bam` (`-r yes`) or `.fastq.gz` (`-r no`) files via `-i`, or use the config-based wrapper (`bash ./STRspy_run_v2.0_Args.sh -i config/InputConfig.txt -t config/UserToolsConfig.txt -j normal` after editing `config/InputConfig.txt`). ## InputConfig.txt INPUT_DIR : A dir must have either fastq (Oxford nanopore genomic reads) or bam (aligned genomic reads such as from PacBio) INPUT_BAM : Given inputs are bam or fastq (yes or no) READ_TYPE : Sequencing Technology (ont or pb) STR_FASTA : A dir contains Fasta files for each STR region of interest [assimung it has flanking regions (+/-) of 500bp] STR_BED : A dir contains Bed files for each STR region of interest [assimung it has flanking regions (+/-) of 500bp] GENOME_FASTA: Genome fasta (hg19/hg38) must provide in case of fastq input. REGION_BED : All STr\R bed has to concatenate into a single bed file to calculate the coverage of it from the alignment sample file. NORM_CUTOFF : A normalization threshold is required to select the top two allles of a STR OUTPUT_DIR : A empty directory to write the results THREADS : Number of memory should be used (default = 1) ## ToolsConfig.txt `GenerateToolConfig.sh` writes this file, so there is normally no reason to edit it by hand. Each value is read with `grep` and `cut -d '='`, so it has to follow the `=` with no space or tab around it: earlier versions of this page showed the names padded with tabs, which leaves the tab inside the path and the tool is then not found. `SEQKIT` is written for completeness and is not read by the core scripts. ``` BEDTOOLS=/user/path/bedtools MINIMAP=/user/path/minimap2 SAMTOOLS=/user/path/samtools XATLAS=/user/path/xatlas PARALLEL=/user/path/parallel SEQKIT=/user/path/seqkit ``` ## Getting help **bash strspy/STRspy_run_v2.0_Args.sh -h** ``` _____ _______ _____ / ____|__ __| __ \ | (___ | | | |__) |___ _ __ _ _ \___ \ | | | _ // __| '_ \| | | | ____) | | | | | \ \\__ \ |_) | |_| | |_____/ |_| |_| \_\___/ .__/ \__, | | | __/ | |_| |___/ =============================================== _ _ __ __ _ _____ _______ _____ __ _ _ _ /\ | | | | / _| / _| (_) / ____|__ __| __ \ / _(_) (_) / \ | |_ ___ ___ | | | |_ ___ _ __ | |_ ___ _ __ ___ _ __ ___ _ ___ | (___ | | | |__) | _ __ _ __ ___ | |_ _| |_ _ __ __ _ / /\ \ | __/ _ \ / _ \| | | _/ _ \| '__| | _/ _ \| '__/ _ \ '_ \/ __| |/ __| \___ \ | | | _ / | '_ \| '__/ _ \| _| | | | '_ \ / _` | / ____ \ | || (_) | (_) | | | || (_) | | | || (_) | | | __/ | | \__ \ | (__ ____) | | | | | \ \ | |_) | | | (_) | | | | | | | | | (_| | /_/ \_\ \__\___/ \___/|_| |_| \___/|_| |_| \___/|_| \___|_| |_|___/_|\___| |_____/ |_| |_| \_\ | .__/|_| \___/|_| |_|_|_|_| |_|\__, | | | __/ | |_| |___/ #^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^Welcome to STRspy^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^# # Analysis : Finding forensic STRs in a Long Read Sample # Requested Citation : https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fsigen.2021.102629 # Author : bioinforupesh2009 DOT au AT gmail DOT com # Copyright (c) : 2021 Kesharwani RK #^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^# Usage: bash STRspy_run_v2.0_Args.sh [-h] [-i -t -j] -- This script is wrapper of STRspy [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fsigen.2021.102629] where: -h show the help -i input config (InputConfig.txt) -t tools config (ToolsConfig.txt) -j job type (parallel/normal) [default: normal] ``` ### Core scripts **bash strspy/src/STRspy_Normal_v2.0_Args.sh -h** ``` #^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^Welcome to STRspy^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^# # Analysis : Finding forensic STRs in a Long Read Sample # Requested Citation : https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms27041889 # Author : bioinforupesh2009 DOT au AT gmail DOT com # Copyright (c) : 2026 Kesharwani RK #^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^# Usage: bash STRspy_Normal_v2.0_Args.sh [-h] [-s -r -t -f -b -g -l -k -o -c -d] -- This script is core-method of STRspy2.0 [https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms27041889] where: -h show the help -s input read dir (either bam or fastq) -r is input bam? (yes/no) -t technology type (ont/pb) -f dir of database fasta -b dir of database bed -g genome fasta file (fa) -l a file of known regions (bed) -k cutoff to find top two alleles (Any value from 0.1 to 0.9) [default: 0.4] -o results dir -c a file of tools config -d Number of threads to use ``` **bash strspy/src/STRspy_Parallel_v2.0_Args.sh -h** ``` #^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^Welcome to STRspy^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^# # Analysis : Finding forensic STRs in a Long Read Sample # Requested Citation : https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms27041889 # Author : bioinforupesh2009 DOT au AT gmail DOT com # Copyright (c) : 2026 Kesharwani RK #^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^# Usage: bash STRspy_Parallel_v2.0_Args.sh [-h] [-s -r -t -f -b -g -l -k -o -c] -- This script is core-method of STRspy2.0 [https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms27041889] where: -h show the help -s input read dir (either bam or fastq) -r is input bam? (yes/no) -t technology type (ont/pb) -f dir of database fasta -b dir of database bed -g genome fasta file (fa) -l a file of known regions (bed) -k cutoff to find top two alleles (Any value from 0.1 to 0.9) [default: 0.4] -o results dir -c a file of tools config -d Num of Threads ``` ## Results from the publication ![](figs/fig2.png)

Figure 2. Read mapping statistics for MinION sequencing runs. Bar plots showing the proportion of passed reads that were STR-mapped (on-target), off-target, and unmapped for the (a), control multiplexes and (b), casework-relevant samples. Each plot shows samples loaded onto a single MinION flow cell. Libraries in the control multiplex are labeled according to sample letter and barcode. A (NIST A), B (NIST B), C (NIST C), M (2800 M).

![](figs/fig3.png)

Figure 3. STRspy2.0 can resolve isoalleles within and between individuals. Allelic balance for autosomal and Y-STR isoalleles detected across control samples in the multiplexing experiment. Each colored bar represents a distinct sequence-based isoallele. Isoallele pairs are shown as blue/orange (pair 1) and green/pink (pair 2) for each locus. Heterozygous alleles that are not in the isoallele pair are colored grey, and samples without isoalleles at a given locus are not shown. Libraries are labeled according to sample letter, barcode, and multiplex size. A (NIST A), B (NIST B), C (NIST C), and M (2800 M).

![](figs/fig4.png)

Figure 4. STRspy2.0 can resolve isoalleles in challenging casework-relevant samples. Normalized read counts for sequence-based alleles detected at D2S1338, D3S1358, and D21S11 in one bone sample (bone03). The red dashed line indicates the normalization threshold (0.4) used to detect heterozygous alleles.

scope.statement: Independent automated verification of reproducible execution. It confirms the tool installs, runs end-to-end, and produces structurally valid output in a standardized environment.
scope.not: This is not an analytical validation. Genotype accuracy, concordance, forensic suitability, and regulatory compliance are out of scope.
scope.disclaimer: Each result is a dated snapshot, verified on the tool's public repository at a pinned commit. STRhub does not store tool source code.

preparation.without_preparation: The latest tagged release (v1.1.1, commit cbf6500) instructs downloading an old Miniconda installer via wget (README.md, line 27), which cannot be executed literally under the automated profile. On the upstream main branch (STRspy v2.0), the Conda environment omits version pins for samtools and Python (pulling a broken OpenSSL 1.0 samtools build) and the wrapper script expects a directory for -i instead of a single BAM file and fails if the -o directory does not already exist.
why: Replace the manual wget Miniconda installer in README.md with a reproducible Conda environment file (setup/STRspy_2.0_env.yml).
Pin python>=3.9 and samtools>=1.12 in setup/STRspy_2.0_env.yml so Conda does not resolve an outdated OpenSSL 1.0 samtools build.
Update src/STRspy_Normal_v2.0_Args.sh to accept a single BAM file in -i, auto-create the -o output directory, and print locus names instead of GenBank accessions in the Locus column.
preparation.run_cmd: bash src/STRspy_Normal_v2.0_Args.sh -i /path/to/input.bam -r yes -t ont -f db-v2/STRspy2.0-DB-fixed -b db-v2/STRspy2.0-DB-fixed -l db-v2/STRspy_v2.DB.sort.bed -k 0.4 -o Results -c config/UserToolsConfig.txt -d 4

files.replaces: pins python>=3.9 and samtools>=1.12 to avoid broken OpenSSL 1.0 samtools build
supports single-file -i BAM input, creates -o directory automatically, outputs locus names

preparation.fork_note: After applying 3 targeted code fixes in the STRhub reproducibility fork (Tfronta/strspy, commit 14d5494) and pinning python>=3.9 and samtools>=1.12, CI run 44934862541 completed all 5/5 gates and produced 22 forensic STR loci on 1000 Genomes ONT hg38. Because code modifications were required, the official upstream commit remains marked as Manual · Fails.

recommendations: Publish a tagged GitHub release for STRspy v2.0 so users and automated evaluators resolve the maintained version by default instead of v1.1.1 (2021).
Document installation in a single copyable block (`conda env create -f setup/STRspy_2.0_env.yml && conda activate strspy_env`) instead of `wget Miniconda3-py39_4.9.2-Linux-x86_64.sh`.
Pin `python>=3.9` and `samtools>=1.12` in `setup/STRspy_2.0_env.yml` so clean Linux environments do not pull a broken OpenSSL 1.0 samtools binary.
Support passing a single BAM/FASTQ file to `-i` and auto-create the `-o` output directory with `mkdir -p` in `src/STRspy_Normal_v2.0_Args.sh`.
